segment_name: Opening: Fact versus Feeling in Industrial England

questions.question: Caroline, you've said that Rachael's scream — 'O the poor lad, the poor lad!' — is actually *truer* than anything Bounderby has to say. That's a fairly wild claim. What do you mean by that, and can you read us that passage?
questions.intent: Get Woodcourt to articulate her strongest take early — that feeling is epistemically prior to fact — and set up the central tension of the segment

questions.question: James, you heard Caroline. She's saying Rachael's grief is the novel's argument. But you've been calling this book a legal brief — you said something before we started about negligent homicide. Is Rachael's anguish the point, or is it actually a distraction from the real crime Dickens is documenting?
questions.intent: Provoke direct disagreement between Blackstone and Woodcourt over whether emotional response is the argument or a vehicle for a harder material critique

questions.question: Eleanor, I want you to read us the pit shaft sentence — 'Before them, at their very feet, was the brink of a black ragged chasm hidden by the thick grass.' You told me this sentence is doing architectural work. What did you mean by that? Because to me it just reads as very good scary writing.
questions.intent: Get Hartley to unpack her structural reading of the passage and introduce her core claim that form and moral argument are inseparable — also sets up her rebuttal to anyone divorcing symbol from material fact

questions.question: James, Eleanor just said the pit is a fact *and* a feeling simultaneously — that Dickens refuses to let us pull them apart. But you said before we started that it's not poetry, it's negligent homicide. Isn't that exactly the separation Eleanor is warning against?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Blackstone's materialist reading and Hartley's insistence that the novel collapses that very distinction — potential for productive friction or surprising agreement

questions.question: Last one, and I want all three of you on this. Caroline, you called the Mrs. Sparsit lunch line — 'It was a part, at once of her dignity and service, not to lunch' — musical. James called it institutional cruelty. Eleanor called it an entire theory of Victorian class performance. Is it possible you're all describing the same sentence and just refusing to admit it?
questions.intent: Push all three experts toward synthesis or clarify the real fault lines — is the disagreement about what Dickens is doing, or about what matters most? Good closing energy for the segment

steering_notes: The segment has a natural arc: open with feeling (Woodcourt's Rachael claim), challenge it with Blackstone's legalism, then let Hartley's structural argument complicate both. The real productive friction is between Blackstone's 'Dickens as witness/documentarian' and Hartley/Woodcourt's shared sense that the form itself is the argument — though Hartley and Woodcourt differ on whether that's architecture or sensation. Don't let anyone retreat into pure close reading without connecting it to the bigger question: what does Dickens think a fact actually is? Keep energy loose — these three want to argue, let them.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's 'negligent homicide' framing directly challenges Woodcourt's claim that the emotional response is the novel's primary argument — Woodcourt will want to respond that grief and injustice aren't in competition

Hartley and Blackstone are closer than they think on the Mrs. Sparsit line — both resist reading it as pure comedy — but they arrive there differently (Hartley: body as ideology; Blackstone: documented class theatre). Push them to notice this.

Woodcourt's 'Dickens makes us feel it before we understand it' is in productive tension with Hartley's claim that understanding and feeling are the same event in the pit passage — get them to hash that out directly
All three are quoting the same two sentences. That's worth naming on air — ask why those lines in particular, and whether that consensus reveals something about what Dickens actually achieved

questions.question: Eleanor, you said before we started recording that this novel is technically radical and people just don't see it. Make that case. Because when most people think Dickens, they're not thinking about sentence structure—they're thinking plot, characters, sentiment. What's actually happening at the level of the prose that we'd miss if we just read for story?
questions.intent: Open the segment with Eleanor's strongest formal claim—that style IS the subject—and let her read c9:p27 to demonstrate it before the others can push back

questions.question: Caroline, you want to read that Louisa passage aloud—c13:p49, the 'You have been so careful of me' speech. Go ahead. But I want to ask you something before you do: James thinks we should sit with how completely Gradgrind *succeeded* in breaking her. You seem to want something different from that scene. What are you hearing in it that he's not?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read the passage aloud for radio impact, then surface the Blackstone-Woodcourt tension over whether Louisa is broken or ferociously diagnostic

questions.question: James, you've been pretty clear that Stephen's 'muddle' isn't poetic or existential—you've basically said Eleanor and Caroline are both romanticising it. So tell me: what is the muddle, specifically? Because I think you want to name it.
questions.intent: Force Blackstone to his sharpest, most specific claim—that the muddle is the marriage law, a concrete institutional failure—and set up direct conflict with Caroline's reading of Stephen as a man with genuine interiority rather than a legal case study

questions.question: Eleanor, here's what I can't quite resolve. You've described Stephen and Louisa as running in parallel—crushed by different machinery, never meeting. But James would say that parallel is misleading: one of them has legal remedies denied by class, the other is a middle-class woman trapped by philosophy. Is that a meaningful difference, or does the novel actually collapse it?
questions.intent: Create triangular tension between all three experts—Eleanor's formal parallelism versus Blackstone's class-specificity versus Woodcourt's emotional interiority argument—and see if they can be forced to disagree about what the novel is fundamentally doing

questions.question: Last one, and I want all three of you on this. Mrs. Pegler turns up and destroys Bounderby's whole mythology—James says that's Dickens demolishing the ideological justification for cruelty, Eleanor says it's structurally the novel's answer delivered in the language of love, simple syntax and plain words. Caroline, you read it differently from both of them. Who's right, and does it actually matter?
questions.intent: Force a three-way synthesis or blowup on the Bounderby revelation, which all three experts have staked out different positions on, and end the segment with the Mrs. Pegler passage as a closing read

steering_notes: Let the passage readings breathe—Caroline and Eleanor both want to read aloud and that's good radio, don't rush them. The productive fault line is Blackstone's insistence on legal-institutional specificity versus the other two's attention to emotional and formal dimensions. Don't let this become a philosophy seminar; keep pulling it back to what's actually on the page. If the conversation gets too abstract, ask someone to read a line. The Bounderby-Mrs. Pegler revelation is the natural closing note—it's the moment where all three threads (legal, emotional, formal) converge.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's claim that Stephen's muddle names a specific law directly contradicts Caroline's reading of Stephen as a figure of genuine interiority—she thinks he's a man to grieve, Blackstone thinks he's a legal victim. That's a real argument worth surfacing early.

Eleanor's parallel structure argument (Stephen mirrors Louisa formally) is something Blackstone will resist on class grounds—he'll say the parallel is aesthetically neat but politically misleading. Let that fight happen after Eleanor makes her formal case.

Caroline and Eleanor are closer to each other than either is to Blackstone, but they disagree about Louisa: Caroline hears a voice breaking, Eleanor insists the language is ferociously active and diagnostic. That's a subtle but interesting distinction worth drawing out in the middle of the segment.

All three experts quote c24:p53 (Mrs. Pegler) but for completely different reasons—Blackstone for ideological demolition, Eleanor for formal irony and simple syntax as structural answer, Caroline implicitly for emotional truth. The closing question is designed to make that three-way disagreement explicit.

segment_name: Dickens Laughs at His Own Villains

questions.question: Caroline, you said before we started recording that you think the comedy in Hard Times is basically *acoustic*—that you have to hear it to get it. Can you prove that? Pick your best passage and read it to us.
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read the Bounderby genealogy from c4:p19 aloud, demonstrating the rhythm argument in real time and setting up a debate about whether the comedy is formal or ideological

questions.question: James, you're nodding along—but I sense you're not entirely buying what Caroline just said. Because your argument before we started was essentially: yes, it's funny, but the laughter is doing something a bit suspicious. What do you mean by that?
questions.intent: Draw out Blackstone's core provocation—that satire replaces analysis and leaves us feeling superior without understanding—and set it in direct tension with Caroline's celebration of Dickens's comic precision

questions.question: Eleanor, James is basically saying Dickens gives us grotesques instead of arguments. But your read of Gradgrind is that the *grammar* of his sentences is doing something more than mockery—that there's almost empathy in the form itself. Can those two things both be true? Is Dickens simultaneously evading analysis *and* achieving it through syntax?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Blackstone's ideological critique and Hartley's formal reading—get Hartley to defend the pianoforte legs passage or the Gradgrind sentence structures as evidence of something more than caricature

questions.question: Let's go to Mrs. Sparsit soaking wet in the ditch—you called that passage almost Beckett-like, which is a big claim. Can you read us a bit of it and tell me what you mean? Because James thinks Dickens is being almost sadistically cruel there, and Caroline thinks it's one of his great comic set pieces. Where are you?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to read from c21:p100 and triangulate between Blackstone's 'venom' reading and Woodcourt's 'great comedy' reading—force all three experts to stake out a position on what we're supposed to *feel* during that scene

questions.question: James, last word to you on this—you said Bounderby's self-made myth was the dominant ideology of the age, and Dickens ridicules the lie but offers nothing in its place. But isn't that actually Dickens's point? That the myth *is* the crime? Or are you saying a novel has a responsibility to do more than just expose?
questions.intent: Push Blackstone to either defend or complicate his strongest claim—that satirical laughter is a form of evasion—and potentially open a final round where Caroline and Eleanor can respond to whether fiction owes us analysis or only illumination

steering_notes: This segment has real friction built in and should feel like a genuine argument, not a symposium. The key fault line is Blackstone vs. the other two: he thinks the comedy is politically evasive, they think it's formally and emotionally sophisticated. Don't let them talk past each other—push Blackstone to be specific about what 'better' satire would look like, and push Hartley and Woodcourt to acknowledge where the laughter might be doing ideological work. The Mrs. Sparsit passage (c21:p100) is the episode where all three readings collide most productively—steer back to it if energy drops. Keep pushing for passages to be read aloud; the acoustic argument needs to be demonstrated, not just asserted.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's claim that Dickens's satire 'replaces analysis' directly challenges Caroline's celebration of comedic precision—she should be invited to respond immediately after he makes it, not after a new question

Eleanor's 'empathy through form' reading of Gradgrind contradicts Blackstone's 'functional rationalist within industrial capital' reading—these are incompatible and should be put side by side explicitly

Both Caroline and Eleanor describe the Mrs. Sparsit passage as comic and even tender; Blackstone calls it sadistic. This is the sharpest disagreement in the segment and should be staged as a three-way moment, not resolved by the host

Caroline's insistence that Bounderby and Gradgrind are 'tragic figures broken by the system' actually partially agrees with Blackstone's structural critique—flag this unexpected overlap and make them figure out whether they agree or not

questions.question: James, you've said something that I keep coming back to — that Stephen isn't pleading, he's actually making a legal argument. Because most readers, I think, encounter this scene and feel sad for him. You're saying we should feel something different. What should we actually feel?
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to open with his sharpest structural take — Stephen as sociologist, not victim — and set up the central tension of the segment before anyone else speaks

questions.question: Eleanor, you've talked about the *shape* of the prose here — the way Dickens actually constructs Stephen's sentences differently from Bounderby's. Can you read us that passage from c9:p51 and then just show us what you mean? Because I think people might not notice it unless someone points at it.
questions.intent: Get Hartley to read aloud the 'I read in th' papers every Sizes' passage and then demonstrate her architectural argument — sets up the contrast between Stephen's long logical structure and Bounderby's fragments, which Blackstone and Woodcourt can then respond to differently

questions.question: Caroline, you said before we started that there's a risk of making this segment too grim — that actually the scene is funny, that Dickens is almost doing slapstick at the end. Eleanor just gave us the tragedy version. Make the case for the comedy.
questions.intent: Provoke productive contrast between Woodcourt's tonal reading and Hartley's structural-tragic one — get Woodcourt to read the 'swelling at his own portrait' line and defend the comedy as inseparable from the critique, not a relief from it

questions.question: James, you called Bounderby's response in c9:p61 to p63 — 'mind your piece-work' — the novel's most chilling moment, and you said it's chilling precisely because it's *not* melodramatic. But Caroline is basically saying Dickens turns Bounderby into a joke by the end. Are those two readings compatible? Is Bounderby a monster or a clown?
questions.intent: Force a direct exchange between Blackstone's institutional-horror reading of Bounderby and Woodcourt's grotesque-comedy reading — the question has a real answer they'll disagree about and both will want to defend

questions.question: Here's the thing I can't quite resolve, and I want to put it to all three of you but Eleanor I'll start with you — Stephen makes a perfect argument, everyone here agrees on that. And it achieves absolutely nothing. So is this scene actually about the *failure* of language? And if it is, what does Dickens think we should do instead of argue?
questions.intent: Close the segment with the hardest question — draw out the political pessimism underneath all three readings and see if they disagree about whether Dickens offers any exit from the bind, not just for Stephen but for the reader

steering_notes: The big tension in this segment is between three readings that look compatible but actually pull in different directions: Blackstone wants systemic critique and will resist sentimentality; Hartley wants formal-structural analysis and will resist psychologizing; Woodcourt wants tonal complexity (the comedy) and will resist unrelieved grimness. Let them think they agree on Stephen's dignity and then push on what follows from that — they don't agree on Bounderby, they don't agree on what Dickens is asking the reader to *feel*, and they don't agree on whether the scene is despairing or energizing. The portrait line is your best tool: all three want to quote it but for different reasons. Make them fight over it.
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley's claim that Stephen's rhetoric is 'aggressive' and actively 'disassembles' Bounderby's authority sits in direct tension with Blackstone's reading of institutional deafness as total and impenetrable — if Stephen's argument is so powerful, why does Blackstone say the machinery just grinds on regardless? Push this.

Woodcourt explicitly says Dickens is 'angrier at Bounderby than he is sorry for Stephen' — Blackstone will agree on the anger but locate it differently (in the system, not the man), while Hartley will want to reframe it as a formal rather than emotional claim. Three different answers to the same sentence.

All three experts want to read the same passage (c9:p51) but for different reasons — Blackstone for the legal-sociological content, Hartley for the sentence architecture, Woodcourt for the emotional force and the reading-aloud quality. Let each read or quote it and then ask the others whether they heard what the previous person heard.

Hartley's claim that Dickens deliberately withholds Stephen's interiority ('the form resists psychological realism') is a direct challenge to Woodcourt's emphasis on Stephen's dignity and moral clarity as something we feel — find a moment to put that to Woodcourt directly.

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our prep chat that I can't stop thinking about — that Louisa having to *articulate her own destruction* before her father will listen is actually the darkest thing in the book. Can you take us into that speech — c21:p124 — and show us what you mean? Because on the surface it reads as this triumphant moment.
questions.intent: Open with the emotional gut-punch of Louisa's confession and establish the central tension: is this scene redemptive or devastating? Sets up immediate disagreement with Blackstone about what counts as change.

questions.question: James, I know you're going to rain on this parade a little — and I want you to. You've called Gradgrind's redemption a 'confidence trick.' What do you mean by that? Because a lot of readers — a lot of *us* — leave that scene feeling like something real happened.
questions.intent: Draw out Blackstone's sharpest political critique: that emotional education is mistaken for social change. Should provoke Woodcourt (who agrees structurally but for different reasons) and Hartley (who'll want to reframe the whole question).

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to bring you in here because I feel like you'd say both James and Caroline are asking the wrong question — that you're both treating this as a story about outcomes, about what changes or doesn't change, when actually Dickens is doing something stranger. You mentioned the 'stone blind' passage — can you read that and tell us what you think he's actually *building* in this scene?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to read c21:p124 aloud and make her case for Dickens's formal achievement — the paradox-as-argument move. Creates a three-way tension: Woodcourt on tragic cost, Blackstone on political failure, Hartley on structural craft.

questions.question: James, I have to put c8:p34 — Stephen's wife — in front of you, because you flagged this in our chat as the place where Dickens's own biases show through. There's that line: 'so much fouler than that in her moral infamy.' Can you read that? Because Eleanor and Caroline both have strong views on what that passage is *doing*, and I think the three of you actually disagree quite sharply about it.
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation on the Stephen's wife passage. Blackstone will call out Dickens's moralizing of poverty; Hartley will argue it's gothic craft not social commentary; Woodcourt will say the language is confused. Real three-way disagreement.

questions.question: Eleanor, before we close this segment — you said something that's been nagging at me: that the novel's real architecture is built around *silence*, around what can't be said. Sissy's secret knowledge of her father, Louisa's unspoken yearning. So let me push you on this — is the fact that Sissy is barely a speaking presence in her own story a formal achievement, like you're arguing, or is it — as Caroline suggested — its own kind of tragedy? Can both things be true at once?
questions.intent: Bring Sissy back into focus and force a direct engagement between Hartley's formalist reading and Woodcourt's feminist critique. Also lets Blackstone pile in on the question of whose silence the novel values and whose it ignores.

steering_notes: The natural shape of this segment runs hot-to-cold: start with the emotional impact of Louisa's confession, let that generate genuine feeling, then let Blackstone complicate it politically, then use Hartley to reframe the whole thing formally. Don't let the political critique from Blackstone overwhelm the segment early — save his sharpest point (the confidence trick) for after we've all felt the scene's power, so the rug-pull lands harder. Watch for the moment all three start talking about what Sissy's silence *means* — that's the segment's hidden center and the place most likely to produce genuine surprise. Keep quotes short and make sure they actually read the passages aloud rather than paraphrasing.
cross_engagement_targets: Hartley argues the Stephen's wife passage (c8:p34) is gothic craft and narrative machinery; Blackstone thinks it exposes Dickens's own class prejudice; Woodcourt thinks the language is simply morally confused — all three positions are genuinely incompatible and all three have textual evidence. This is the segment's richest point of conflict.

Blackstone says Louisa gains self-knowledge not agency; Woodcourt says she had to be destroyed to be heard; Hartley says the speech is a formal inversion of Gradgrind's logic. They're each responding to a different question, which means they'll talk past each other unless pushed to address the same point directly.

All three experts quote c7:p2 — 'The wretched ignorance with which Jupe clung to this consolation' — but read it completely differently: Blackstone as Dickens's sharpest irony, Woodcourt as the prose enacting its own values, Hartley as proof the irony cuts both ways and we're not supposed to feel clean. Force them to address each other's readings of the same sentence.

segment_name: The Art of Dickens's Social Mirror

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our chat that stuck with me—that the argument of this novel lives in the *rhythm* of the prose, not just the content. Can you make that real for us? Pick a passage and actually read it out loud, and tell us what we'd miss if we just paraphrased it.
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read aloud and demonstrate her core thesis about rhythm-as-argument; sets up the c2:p40 or c18:p55 passages and gives the other two a concrete target to respond to

questions.question: James, I want to push on something. Eleanor and Caroline are both going to talk about how Dickens *crafts* these passages—the syntax, the rhythm, the comedy. But you've been pretty firm that this isn't primarily an aesthetic achievement, it's closer to documentary. So when the gentleman says 'You mustn't fancy' at c2:p40—is Dickens being a great artist there, or is he being a great journalist?
questions.intent: Force the aesthetic-versus-documentary tension into the open; provokes Eleanor who sees pure linguistic critique and Caroline who sees moral rhythm, while drawing out Blackstone's strongest historical-materialist take

questions.question: Eleanor, you've made this case that Dickens's real genius is what he *withholds*—the things characters can't say. You mentioned Stephen's prayer at c18:p55, barely above a breath. What's actually happening technically in that moment? Why does that whisper land harder than a speech would?
questions.intent: Draw out Eleanor's structural-silence argument and get her to read the c18:p55 passage; sets up cross-engagement since Caroline also loves this passage but from a different angle—dignity versus formal suppression

questions.question: Caroline, you flagged Mrs. Sparsit's monologue at c20:p160 as a passage most readers get wrong—they laugh and move on, but you think it's actually quite dark. Make the case. Because James is going to say it's just Dickens skewering class hypocrisy, and Eleanor's going to call it syntactic rope—are you saying there's something sadder going on?
questions.intent: Surface the three-way disagreement about Mrs. Sparsit: comedy vs. critique vs. trapped performance; names the other experts' positions explicitly to provoke rebuttal and keep energy high

questions.question: Last one, and I want all three of you on this. James, you ended our conversation with something a bit alarming—you said the machine Dickens is describing is still running. Eleanor thinks the novel is ultimately about what certain ideologies do to *language*. Caroline thinks it's about what they do to *feeling*. Can those three things—the machine, the language, the feeling—actually be separated? Or is that the argument the novel is making?
questions.intent: Bring all three takes into direct collision for the segment's climax; invites synthesis or productive disagreement and gives each expert a clear lane while forcing them to reckon with each other's frameworks

steering_notes: Keep pushing the experts off abstraction and back to the text—every time someone makes a claim, ask them to read the passage that proves it. The three-way tension is: Blackstone wants to historicize, Hartley wants to formalize, Woodcourt wants to emotionalize. These aren't incompatible but they'll feel like they are, which is good radio. Don't let Mrs. Sparsit become just a comedy bit—Caroline's 'trapped in her own performance' read is the most interesting thing anyone said in pre-interviews and needs air. Watch for the moment when Blackstone calls something reportage and Hartley calls the same thing syntax—that's the flashpoint.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone calls c2:p40 'ideological control as documented practice'; Hartley calls the same passage 'syntax performing self-deception'—get them to argue about whether those readings compete or collapse into each other

Hartley and Woodcourt both love c18:p55 but for different reasons: Hartley sees formal suppression (the parenthetical stage direction as argument), Woodcourt sees Stephen's unbroken dignity in dialect—ask them directly whether those are the same thing

Woodcourt says Bounderby's self-made narrative is 'almost seductive—it nearly works'; Blackstone says Victorian audiences would recognize it as a courtroom defense strategy. Push: if it nearly works AND it's a real legal strategy, does that make the satire less safe than we thought?

All three cite c20:p160 but read it completely differently: Hartley (syntactic rope and craftsmanship), Blackstone (obscene self-pity of the privileged), Woodcourt (genuine sadness, a woman trapped in performance)—this is a three-way split on a single passage and should be staged explicitly

segment_name: Closing: What Hard Times Demands of Us

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our chat that's been rattling around in my head — that Louisa wins the argument but loses the relationship, and that the loss is the *point*. So what exactly is Dickens asking us to do with that? Because it's not a comfortable ending, is it — it's almost cruel.
questions.intent: Open the segment with Caroline's core tragic reading and get her to read from c13:p47 — the 'What do I know' passage — so listeners feel the weight of Louisa's accusation before the debate starts

questions.question: James, you'd push back on that though, right? Because you've been insisting all along that this isn't just about one father and one daughter — Gradgrind isn't a monster, he's a rational man acting in good faith. Does that make it *worse*, or does it let him off the hook?
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to complicate the emotional reading Caroline just offered — draw out his institutional critique and the 'barriers erected' reading of c13:p28, and provoke disagreement about whether Gradgrind deserves sympathy

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to bring you in here because you've been making this argument that the novel isn't really asking us to be better *people* — it's asking us to be better *readers*. Can you show us what you mean? You mentioned this parenthetical that Dickens drops in — something about Gradgrind not seeing what the narrator sees?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to read aloud the 'not to him, for he saw nothing of it' passage and articulate her thesis about Dickens's narrative method — the idea that the parenthetical itself is an act of imagination

questions.question: Right, but James — Eleanor is essentially saying the novel is about *how we read*. You're saying it's about *what we erase*. Those feel like they should agree but I'm not sure they do. When those workers are reading their fables in c6:p4, is that an act of personal imagination or is it an act of political resistance? Does it matter which?
questions.intent: Force a direct engagement between Blackstone's institutional reading and Hartley's narrative reading — use the workers' reading passage as the battleground, get both of them talking to each other rather than at the host

questions.question: Last question, and I want all three of you on this one — Caroline, you start. You said something that I think is the most uncomfortable thing anyone's said to me about this book: that we're all capable of missing the wavering moment when someone needs us. So what does Hard Times actually *demand* of us — not of Gradgrind, not of Victorian education reformers, but of us, right now, today?
questions.intent: Bring the segment home with Caroline's most personal and direct thesis, then let Blackstone and Hartley respond — aim for a moment where all three are genuinely in conversation about what the novel costs the reader personally

steering_notes: Start emotional and let Blackstone's institutional argument complicate it — don't let the conversation stay abstract for long. The three guests have genuine friction: Caroline reads tragedy, James reads politics, Eleanor reads narrative form. The sweet spot is getting them to argue about whether Dickens is demanding personal, political, or readerly transformation — ideally all at once. Push for passages to be read aloud wherever possible; the rhythm of c13:p47 and the parenthetical in the 'not to him' passage will do more work than any paraphrase. Watch for the moment when Blackstone and Hartley's readings collide over the workers' passage — that's the best cross-engagement in the segment. Don't over-resolve: let the ending feel genuinely open, because the novel does.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's claim that Gradgrind is rational and well-intentioned directly challenges Caroline's tragic framing — if he's not a villain, is the loss still a tragedy or just an error? Push them to argue this out after question 2.

Hartley's 'better readers' thesis and Blackstone's 'weaponized reason' thesis sound compatible but actually compete — Hartley locates the demand in the reader's attention, Blackstone locates it in institutional structures. The workers' reading passage (c6:p4) is the flashpoint: defiant imagination or political act? Use question 4 to force this.

Caroline's insistence that the novel is about irreversible damage sits in tension with Hartley's more ambiguous reading — Hartley thinks Dickens doesn't resolve whether understanding without transformation is enough; Caroline thinks the point is precisely that it isn't enough. Get them to name that disagreement directly after question 3.
